notes: Cases whose id starts with 'real-' were added to make the corpus resemble what is actually posted, not what is easy to synthesize. Their mix follows an ecosystem census of real usenet archives covering 890,852 releases / 79.6 TB across the two busiest movie and TV groups, plus archive headers read from roughly a thousand real posts.

Census weighting: multi-volume RAR carries 84% of all data (only 2.5% of releases by count). Within multi-volume, 84% is STORED with no compression and 14% is ENCRYPTED - together 98.6%. Compressed is 1.4%. Solid archives were extinct in the sample: zero out of ~700 archives read.

So the flagship realism cases are multi-volume store-mode media-class archives, followed by encrypted store-mode multi-volume. Encryption scales with release size (1-5 GB: 2% encrypted; 20-60 GB: 33%; >60 GB: 49%), which is why the encrypted cases are store-mode multi-volume rather than compressed.

The compressed source-text, machine-code, and mixed cases are the 1.4% minority by data, but they are the classes that carry LZ match-length distribution: they exist to measure window-copy behavior on real code, real text, and real machine code, not because they are common.
No new solid cases were added: solid is extinct in the wild, and the pre-existing solid cases already cover the format for correctness.

BLAKE2sp (-htb) cases are present regardless of prevalence, under the standing requirement that this decoder be best in class for every archive that can exist. Member sizes are chosen so at least one blake2 case sits well above the parallel hash pipeline's 8 MiB per-member threshold and one sits below it.

The media class is TRUE VIDEO: real muxed A/V encoded by ffmpeg (libx264/AAC into Matroska, plus one libx265/AAC into MP4) inside a digest-pinned encoder image, single-threaded and bitexact so the bytes are reproducible forever. That is what actually rides inside a scene RAR. The older synthesized high-entropy 'media' profile stays in the schema as the generic fallback and is still used where a member has to land on an exact byte count, which an encoder cannot do.
For ffmpeg-video cases payload_bytes is a TARGET: the generator converts it to an encode duration and records whatever size the encoder actually produced. Every other profile hits its size exactly.

PAYLOAD POLICY: video payloads belong to store-mode (uncompressed) cases only. Compressed (normal-mode) cases must carry genuinely compressible payloads - the text, source-text, machine-code, and mixed classes - so they actually exercise the LZ path and produce a meaningful comparison against the oracle. A compressed case whose payload defeats the compressor measures nothing.

Why that policy exists, measured: a 'compression attempted over real video' case (real-media-normal-v7) was built and then removed, because rar refuses to compress real x264 output. Given -m3 over a real H.264/AAC MKV the writer auto-selected stored for that member - unrar reports 'Compression: RAR 5.0(v50) -m0', ratio 100%, packed size equal to unpacked size - so only the 64 KiB .nfo sidecar ever reached the LZ window (65,536 bytes, against 33,554,432 for the older synthesized high-entropy payload). The case measured the store path while claiming to benchmark compression, and duplicated the store-mode cases that already cover it. Real posted media therefore does zero window-copy work in EVERY mode, stored or nominally compressed.

Realistic payload classes are byte-identical across the cases that share a class, so writer, mode, and checksum variants are compared with the data held constant. See internal/bench/payload.go for how each class is derived from pinned inputs.
